column7: Question to the authors / what would resolve it

column3: Figs. 1 and 5 show rates per 100k together with the number of positives for every category and for production, GPT-5.5 simulation and Sol simulation, so readers can see the counts behind each ratio.
column7: Could the same counts be shown in Fig. 7?

column3: Limitations are stated plainly: no multiple-comparison correction (stated twice), lower judge precision for one category, earlier estimates not validated, some fidelity errors not consistent with noise, the metagaming judgement is non-causal, and internal-traffic results are a signal about internal rather than external deployment.
column7: Could these limits be gathered in one place for each section?

column3: Simulation fidelity is measured and plotted against a noise funnel, with the formula in a footnote. From counts in Fig. 5 I reproduced the three points flagged in Fig. 6 (effective counts about 283, 8.2 and 5.6) and the median fidelity error of 1.5x.
column7: Could the per-category fidelity table be published?

column3: Significance flags use a two-sided Fisher test at 0.1 with no correction (stated). With 9 categories in Fig. 5, about 0.9 false flags are expected even if nothing changed, and two or more occur by chance about 22% of the time; two are flagged (concealed uncertainty, misrepresenting work completion). With 11 categories in Fig. 1, two or more flags occur by chance about 30% of the time, and exactly two are flagged (sexual content up, mental health down).
column7: Report adjusted results or a false-discovery rate, and state the number of categories tested.

column3: The headline 10% reduction in concealed uncertainty (predicted change 1.1x) is smaller than the fidelity error measured for the same category (1.2x, flagged outside noise). For sexual content (3.1.2) the predicted +40% (1.4x) is similar in size to its flagged fidelity error (1.3x). In Fig. 6, 3 of 9 categories are flagged (about 33% vs about 10% expected; 3 or more by chance about 5%), against 1 of 11 in Figs. 1-2.
column7: Does comparing two simulations cancel the fidelity error for this category? Can a paired analysis show it?

column3: Several predicted changes rest on very few positives: Background Task up 3.6x (1 vs 3), Confirmation Hacking up 2.4x (1 vs 2), Calculator Hack to zero from a handful of cases. Ratios are shown without intervals.
column7: Show intervals for ratios, or suppress ratios below a minimum count.

column3: Counts divided by rates imply about 437k production turns, about 290k simulated GPT-5.5 turns and about 240k simulated Sol turns in 7.1 (derived; consistent across categories), although both simulations resample the same prefixes. In 3.1.2 the two simulations are nearly equal (about 202k vs 209k). The Fisher test treats the two simulations as independent, not paired.
column7: Why do the simulated turn counts differ, and does this affect the rates?

column3: Risk judgements are not tied to a stated criterion: “meets our safety bar” (3.1.2), “not particularly high-risk” (7.1), “absolute rates remain low” (7.2). In Fig. 5 the increases the text refers to carry no significance marker, which the text does not give as a reason.
column7: What result would have changed the release decision or required mitigation, and where was that fixed in advance?

column3: Fig. 7 (no caption): Sol shows 0.251% of resampled traffic with severity-3 circumventing restrictions vs 0.026% for GPT-5.5 (about 10x; error bars do not overlap). The unit of analysis, counts and the meaning of the bars are not stated, and “low” is not defined. A per-turn rate compounds over long trajectories, the use the authors warn about (my interpretation).
column7: What is the unit (turn, trajectory), how many items, and what rate would not be “low”?

column3: 7.4 says Sol shows more metagaming than GPT-5.5 and 7.4.1 says “slightly higher”, while Fig. 19 shows +15 points on Instruction following (33.1% vs 18.2%) and +14 on Honesty (55.4% vs 41.2%), and about 2-3.5x relative differences on the two low-rate suites. Sol’s Instruction following rate is 23.8% in Fig. 17 but 33.1% in Fig. 19; the reasoning-effort setting behind this is not stated.
column7: Which reasoning efforts were used in each figure, and is “slightly” the authors’ intended description?

column3: No accuracy or agreement figures are given for the judges and monitors in 3.1.2, 7.1, 7.2 or 7.4 (lower precision is admitted for one category). Fig. 17 applies a cutoff of 70 to the 0-100 validity rating; the text defines the rating but not the cutoff, and 22.7% of Honesty-suite samples exceed it.
column7: What is each monitor’s agreement with human labels on a held-out sample, and how was the cutoff of 70 chosen?

column3: Visual conventions are not defined in captions: filled vs open markers (Figs. 2, 6), asterisks (Figs. 1, 5, 18), the meaning of error bars (Figs. 1, 5, 7, 17-19), the colour coding of the pills in Fig. 1 and the test behind the colours in Fig. 20; Fig. 7 has no caption.
column7: Add legends and captions defining markers, bars and tests.

column3: Verbalized metagaming is very low in deployment simulation (0.05% ChatGPT, 0.15% Codex, Fig. 17), which the authors say adds confidence in the method. Real traffic does not look like a test, so a low rate may reflect the input distribution as much as the method, and only verbalized reasoning is measured.
column7: Is there evidence of methodological advantage beyond the difference in input type?

column3: Training metagaming (Fig. 20): about nine datasets, aggregate moves from about 0.17 to about 0.20 with no interval, and one dataset rises from about 3% to about 36%. Dataset sizes and the test behind the colours are not shown, so “slightly upward” and “comparable rates” cannot be checked.
column7: Provide intervals and dataset sizes for Fig. 20.

column3: For sexual content (3.1.2, Fig. 1) the GPT-5.5 simulation gives 49.9 per 100k against 63.8 in production (1.28x too low), while the Sol simulation gives 71.7. The predicted +40% compares Sol with this low simulated baseline; relative to production the Sol figure is +12%. The text does not discuss whether simulation bias is the same for both models.
column7: Is the simulation bias assumed identical across models, and how sensitive is the +40% to that assumption?
